title: Indra's lessons: the self through waking, dream and sleep
hookLine: Indra keeps going back to Prajapati until he learns the self that stays through waking, dream and deep sleep.
carry: the witness self stays through waking, dream and sleep
tomorrow: a father weeps for a son who's alive and well. why?

lines: LOOK IN A PAN OF WATER.
cards: The gods and the demons both hear it: there's a self that never ages, never dies, never grieves, and whoever finds it gains everything. Each side sends its best.
Indra comes for the gods, Virochana for the demons, and they live as students with Prajapati, the creator, for thirty-two years. Then he tells them: look in a pan of water. What you see is the self.
Virochana goes home happy; the self is the body. Indra stops on the road. If the body is dressed up, so is the reflection.
If the body is hurt, so is the reflection. That can't be it. He goes back.

teach.h: THE BODY? THE DREAMER? DEEP SLEEP?
teach.b: Again and again. Prajapati offers the one who moves about in dreams; Indra objects that a dreamer can still be chased, and weep. Then the one in deep, dreamless sleep; Indra objects that there, it knows nothing at all.

teach.h: THE BODY DIES; THE SELF DOESN'T.
teach.b: In all, the story says, he stays a hundred and one years, until Prajapati teaches that the body is mortal, and the self that dwells in it is not. That's the Chandogya Upanishad.
The Panchadashi, a book of Advaita verses tradition credits to Vidyaranya, opens on the same three states.

teach.h: THE SOUNDS DIFFER; THE KNOWING DOESN'T.
teach.b: In waking, sounds and sights differ, but the knowing of them is one. In dreams the objects change, and the knowing is the same. And deep sleep?
On waking you say, I slept and knew nothing. Someone was there to know the nothing.
Advaita teachers call this the sakshi, the witness: the self that watches waking, dream and sleep, and neither rises nor sets.
Many teachers put it simply: moods, roles and years come and go, and the one who notices them doesn't. A neighbor tradition sings something close.

teach.h: THE PSALM: THOU ART THE SAME.
teach.b: A psalm in the Hebrew Bible, in the King James Version, says of the earth and heavens: "as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed: But thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end."
Shared: everything seen changes, and something doesn't. The honest difference: the psalm says it to God, a thou the singer trusts.

teach.h: SAID TO GOD, OR FOUND AS THE SELF.
teach.b: The Panchadashi finds the unchanging as awareness, a person's own self.

how: Advaita teachers tell Indra's story from the Chandogya Upanishad and teach the Panchadashi's opening on waking, dream and deep sleep to point students to the witness self, often with a teacher. Psalm 102 is part of the Hebrew Bible, read by Jews and Christians.

games.q: Indra's search, the opening, and a neighbor. tap the pairs.
p: took the body for the self
went back until he learned the self

s: Indra took the first answer and went home happy
that was Virochana. Indra saw the reflection changes with the body, and went back.
the book uses deep sleep as evidence that awareness was there
on waking a person says, I slept and knew nothing. who knew the nothing?
the psalm and the Panchadashi say the same thing in different words
both hold something unchanging; the psalm says it to God, the Panchadashi finds it as awareness, the self.

games.q: you wake up and say: I slept well and knew nothing at all. what does the Panchadashi hear in that sentence?
o: someone was there to know the nothing: awareness didn't switch off.
the mind was simply gone, and there's nothing more to it.
a dream you've forgotten, so nothing can be learned.
games.why: The verses ask who was there to know the nothing. So the knowing was there through waking, dream and deep sleep, neither rising nor setting.

practice: Listen for the sounds around you, one at a time: a hum, a car, a voice, your own breath. Let each one arrive and fade without following it.
Then, between sounds, notice the hearing itself, there before the next one comes, still there after it goes. Advaita teachers call this resting as the witness.

wordCard.voice: The Panchadashi: a book of Advaita verses that opens where Indra's search ended. Sounds change; the knowing of them stays one.

orig.note: Sanskrit Panchadashi, the name of this book of Advaita verses credited by tradition to Vidyaranya.

carryVoice: Your line, from Indra's long search: the witness self stays through waking, dream and sleep. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7–8.12 (Indra and Virochana live with Prajapati; the self in the reflection, the dreamer, the one in deep sleep; Indra's objections; a hundred and one years; the body mortal, the self bodiless and immortal)

Panchadashi 1.3–7 (Tattva-viveka: objects of waking differ, consciousness of them does not; the same in dream; in deep sleep, remembered on waking; consciousness neither rises nor sets and is self-luminous)
